choices.text: The larger pot is at a higher temperature because it holds more water.

choices.text: They are at the same temperature, but the larger pot has more thermal energy.

choices.text: They have the same thermal energy because they are at the same temperature.

choices.text: The small pot has more thermal energy because its water came to a boil sooner.

questions.explanation: Temperature tells the average energy of motion of the particles, and both pots boil at the same temperature. Thermal energy is a total, so it grows with the number of particles. The larger pot has the same average but many more molecules, so it holds more thermal energy.
questions.misconception: A larger amount of a substance must be at a higher temperature, or equal temperatures mean equal thermal energy.
questions.hint: One of these quantities is an average, and one is a total.

choices.text: The mug's molecules move faster on average, but the pitcher holds more thermal energy.

choices.text: Pouring out half of the water

questions.prompt: Scientists use the word heat only for energy that is moving from warmer to cooler. Which sentences use heat the way a scientist would? Select all that apply.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Scientists use the word heat only for energy that is moving from warmer to cooler. Which sentences use heat the way a scientist would? Select all that apply. The sentences are: this mug of cocoa has a lot of heat stored in it; heat flowed from the hot soup into the cold metal spoon; the heat outside today is 35 degrees; the burner transferred heat to the pan because the burner was hotter; and the ice cube's heat flowed into my hand and made it feel cold.

choices.text: This mug of cocoa has a lot of heat stored in it.
choices.rationale: What the cocoa stores is thermal energy; it becomes heat only when it moves into something cooler.

choices.text: Heat flowed from the hot soup into the cold metal spoon.
choices.rationale: Correct: energy is moving from a warmer object to a cooler one, which is exactly what heat means.

choices.text: The heat outside today is 35 degrees.
choices.rationale: A reading in degrees is a temperature, not heat.

choices.text: The burner transferred heat to the pan because the burner was hotter.
choices.rationale: Correct: energy passes from the hotter burner to the cooler pan because of their temperature difference.

choices.text: The ice cube's heat flowed into my hand and made it feel cold.
choices.rationale: Heat flows from warmer to cooler, so energy flowed from your hand into the ice; your hand feels cold because it is losing energy.

questions.explanation: In everyday speech, heat can mean temperature or the energy something holds. In science, heat is only the energy moving from a warmer object to a cooler one. The soup and burner sentences describe energy in transit. The cocoa sentence describes stored thermal energy, the weather sentence describes temperature, and heat never flows from the cold ice into a warmer hand.
questions.misconception: Objects contain heat, heat and temperature mean the same thing, or heat can flow out of a colder object.

choices.text: Each molecule has grown larger.
choices.rationale: Warming makes molecules move faster; it does not change their size.

choices.text: On average, they are moving faster than before.
choices.rationale: Correct: for the same substance, a higher temperature means a higher average speed.

choices.text: There are more water molecules in the glass now.
choices.rationale: Warming adds energy, not molecules; the amount of water stayed the same.

choices.text: Their average kinetic energy is greater than before.
choices.rationale: Correct: temperature measures average kinetic energy, so a rise means a bigger average.

choices.text: Every molecule now moves at exactly the same speed.
choices.rationale: Molecules always have a spread of speeds; temperature reports their average.

questions.conditions: Same glass of water, which stays liquid.
questions.explanation: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of a substance's particles. When the reading rises, the water molecules are moving faster on average. They do not get bigger or multiply, and they still move at many different speeds.
questions.misconception: Warming makes particles grow, or every particle in a sample moves at the same speed.
questions.hint: Temperature is about how the particles move, not about their size or number.

questions.prompt: Ice cubes are moved from a −18 °C freezer into a −5 °C freezer. They warm to −5 °C but do not melt. What changed for their water molecules?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Ice cubes are moved from a freezer at minus 18 degrees Celsius into a freezer at minus 5 degrees Celsius. They warm to minus 5 degrees but do not melt. What changed for their water molecules?

choices.text: They vibrate harder, but stay in their fixed positions.
choices.rationale: Correct: a higher temperature means more energetic vibration, and the ice is still solid, so the molecules stay locked in place.

choices.text: They started moving for the first time, after being perfectly still.
choices.rationale: Solid particles were already vibrating at −18 °C; colder ice has gentler vibrations, not none.

choices.text: They now slide past one another, even though the ice has not melted.
choices.rationale: Sliding past one another is how particles move in a liquid; the cubes are still solid ice.

choices.text: Nothing changed, because all ice below 0 °C is the same inside.
choices.rationale: A temperature rise always means more energetic particle motion, even in a solid that stays below its melting point.

questions.explanation: Water molecules in ice are locked in fixed positions, but they always vibrate. When the ice warms from −18 °C to −5 °C, its molecules gain energy and vibrate more strongly in the same spots. They break free and slide past one another only once the ice reaches its melting point and keeps taking in energy.
questions.misconception: Particles in a cold solid do not move, or a solid's particles cannot change their motion unless it melts.
questions.hint: What does a rising temperature tell you about how particles move, even in a solid?

evidence.supports: As ice gains thermal energy, its water molecules vibrate faster and faster within their fixed positions and the ice's temperature rises before it melts.
In a solid, particles are locked in place and move only by vibrating within the fixed arrangement.

evidence.locator: Section 1, Thermal Energy and Temperature (margin note)
evidence.supports: A rise in temperature means the molecules have sped up.

questions.prompt: Two objects at different temperatures are touching. On its own, in which overall direction does energy move between them as heat?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Two objects at different temperatures are touching. On its own, in which overall direction does energy move between them as heat?

choices.text: From the cooler object to the warmer object
choices.rationale: This is the 'cold flows' idea; cold is not a substance, and the net energy flow goes the other way.

choices.text: From the bigger object to the smaller object, whatever their temperatures
choices.rationale: Size does not set the direction; a small hot nail dropped in a big bucket of cool water still warms the water.

choices.text: From the warmer object to the cooler object
choices.rationale: Correct: on average the warmer object's particles have more energy of motion, so collisions pass more energy to the cooler object's particles than comes back.

choices.text: From the object with more thermal energy to the one with less
choices.rationale: A lukewarm bathtub has more thermal energy than a hot cup of tea, yet a cup set in the bath still loses energy to the bath water; temperature decides the direction.

questions.explanation: Heat flows from warmer to cooler on its own. Particles in the warmer object have more energy of motion on average, so in collisions they hand more energy to the cooler object's particles than they get back. The flow continues until the temperatures are equal.
questions.misconception: Cold flows into warm objects, or energy flows from the object with more thermal energy.
questions.hint: Which object's particles have more energy of motion on average?

evidence.locator: Section 1, Transferring Thermal Energy as Heat
evidence.supports: Collisions between particles move thermal energy out of the warmer object into the cooler one, and this continues until their temperatures match.

choices.rationale: Particles at 8 °C are still moving quickly; equal temperatures do not freeze their motion.

choices.text: They still collide and trade energy, but equal amounts go each way.

questions.explanation: Once two objects reach the same temperature, their particles keep moving and colliding. In those collisions, as much energy passes from stone to water as from water to stone. With no net transfer, both temperatures stay at 8 °C.
